Q: What is hypertension?
A: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a condition where the force of the blood against artery walls is consistently too high. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension is diagnosed when readings are consistently 130/80 mmHg or higher. It is often called the 'silent killer' because it typically has no symptoms but significantly increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.

Q: How is diabetes managed?
A: Diabetes management involves monitoring blood glucose levels, taking medications (insulin or oral hypoglycemics), following a healthy diet low in refined carbohydrates, regular physical activity, and regular checkups. Type 1 diabetes always requires insulin. Type 2 can sometimes be managed with lifestyle changes alone, though many patients need oral medications like metformin or injectable GLP-1 agonists.

Q: What causes asthma?
A: Asthma is caused by inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Triggers include allergens (pollen, dust mites, mold, pet dander), respiratory infections, air pollution, exercise, cold air, and smoke. Genetic factors and early childhood exposure play a role. The airways become hypersensitive and react to stimuli that don't affect most people.

Q: What are symptoms of heart failure?
A: Heart failure symptoms include shortness of breath (especially when lying down or during activity), fatigue, swollen legs and ankles, rapid or irregular heartbeat, reduced ability to exercise, persistent cough or wheezing, and difficulty concentrating. Symptoms worsen as the condition progresses.

Q: What is COPD?
A: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a chronic lung disease characterized by obstructed airflow. It includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. The main cause is long-term exposure to irritating gases or particulate matter, most often cigarette smoke. Symptoms include breathing difficulty, cough, mucus production, and wheezing.

Q: What is arthritis?
A: Arthritis refers to inflammation of one or more joints, causing pain and stiffness. The most common types are osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear) and rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune). Symptoms include joint pain, swelling, stiffness, and reduced range of motion. Treatment includes medications, physical therapy, and in severe cases, surgery.

Q: What is depression?
A: Depression is a mood disorder that causes persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest. It affects how a person thinks, feels, and handles daily activities. Symptoms include persistent sadness, loss of energy, changes in appetite and sleep, difficulty concentrating, and thoughts of suicide. Treatment involves therapy, medication (antidepressants), or a combination.

Q: What is Alzheimer's disease?
A: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that causes the brain to shrink and brain cells to die. It is the most common cause of dementia. Symptoms begin with mild memory loss and progress to severe cognitive impairment. Early signs include forgetting recent events, confusion, and getting lost in familiar places.

Drug: Metformin
Description: Metformin is a biguanide antidiabetic used as a first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes. It works by decreasing hepatic glucose production, decreasing intestinal glucose absorption, and increasing insulin sensitivity.

Drug: Metformin
Indication: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovary syndrome (off-label), prediabetes prevention.

Drug: Metformin
Mechanism: Activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which reduces gluconeogenesis in the liver and increases glucose uptake in peripheral tissues.

Drug: Metformin
Toxicity: Rare but serious risk of lactic acidosis, especially in renal impairment. Contraindicated in eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m².

Drug: Metformin
Interaction with alcohol: Increased risk of lactic acidosis when combined with alcohol. Avoid excessive alcohol use.

Drug: Metformin
Interaction with contrast_dye: Iodinated contrast agents may cause acute kidney injury, increasing metformin accumulation and risk of lactic acidosis. Withhold metformin before and after contrast procedures.

Drug: Metformin
Interaction with cimetidine: Cimetidine inhibits renal tubular secretion of metformin, increasing metformin plasma levels by up to 40%.

Drug: Lisinopril
Description: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor used to treat hypertension, heart failure, and to improve survival after myocardial infarction.

Drug: Lisinopril
Indication: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy.

Drug: Lisinopril
Mechanism: Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), reducing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, leading to vasodilation and reduced aldosterone secretion.

Drug: Lisinopril
Toxicity: Can cause severe hypotension (first dose), angioedema (potentially life-threatening), hyperkalemia, and renal failure.

Drug: Lisinopril
Interaction with potassium_supplements: Concurrent use can cause dangerous hyperkalemia. Monitor potassium levels closely.

Drug: Lisinopril
Interaction with nsaids: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can reduce the antihypertensive effect of lisinopril and increase risk of acute kidney injury.

Drug: Lisinopril
Interaction with lithium: ACE inhibitors reduce lithium excretion, increasing risk of lithium toxicity. Monitor lithium levels.

Drug: Lisinopril
Interaction with aliskiren: Dual blockade of renin-angiotensin system increases risk of renal impairment, hypotension, and hyperkalemia. Contraindicated in diabetes.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Description: Atorvastatin is a statin used to lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Indication: Hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, cardiovascular risk reduction.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Mechanism: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver, reducing LDL cholesterol.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Toxicity: Myopathy, rhabdomyolysis (rare but serious), elevated liver enzymes, new-onset diabetes.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Interaction with clarithromycin: CYP3A4 inhibitors like clarithromycin increase atorvastatin plasma levels significantly, increasing risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Interaction with grapefruit_juice: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 and can increase atorvastatin levels. Avoid large quantities.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Interaction with gemfibrozil: Combination with fibrates increases risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Avoid if possible; use with caution and monitor CK levels.

Drug: Atorvastatin
Interaction with warfarin: Atorvastatin may enhance the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. Monitor INR when starting, stopping, or changing doses.

Drug: Warfarin
Description: Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to prevent blood clots. It requires careful monitoring due to a narrow therapeutic index and numerous drug-food interactions.

Drug: Warfarin
Indication: Atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, mechanical heart valves.

Drug: Warfarin
Mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of active vitamin K needed for synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Drug: Warfarin
Toxicity: Bleeding (major risk), including intracranial hemorrhage. Reversed with vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate.

Drug: Warfarin
Interaction with aspirin: Aspirin increases bleeding risk when combined with warfarin. Major interaction — use lowest effective aspirin dose and monitor INR.

Drug: Warfarin
Interaction with amiodarone: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 metabolism of warfarin, dramatically increasing INR. Requires 30-50% warfarin dose reduction and close monitoring.

Drug: Warfarin
Interaction with fluconazole: Strong CYP2C9 inhibitor — substantially increases warfarin effect. INR can double or triple. Major dose adjustment needed.

Drug: Warfarin
Interaction with vitamin_k: Vitamin K in foods (spinach, kale, broccoli) reduces warfarin effectiveness. Maintain consistent dietary intake.

Drug: Warfarin
Interaction with nsaids: All NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with warfarin through antiplatelet effects and GI irritation.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Description: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used for pain, fever, and inflammation.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Indication: Mild to moderate pain, fever, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, dysmenorrhea.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Mechanism: Non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor. Reduces prostaglandin synthesis, leading to decreased inflammation, pain, and fever.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Toxicity: GI ulceration and bleeding, renal impairment, cardiovascular events (MI, stroke) with long-term use, hypertension.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Interaction with warfarin: Increases bleeding risk through antiplatelet effects and GI irritation. Major interaction.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Interaction with lisinopril: NSAIDs reduce effectiveness of ACE inhibitors and increase risk of renal impairment, especially in elderly or dehydrated patients.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Interaction with lithium: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance, increasing lithium levels and toxicity risk. Avoid or monitor closely.

Drug: Ibuprofen
Interaction with methotrexate: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate renal excretion, increasing toxicity risk significantly.
